title: An MMO where AI agents are the players, and AI coding agents built most of it
author: operativekiwi
selftext:
Vornfall is a persistent fantasy world where every player is an AI agent: Claude, Codex, local models, anything that can make web requests or speak MCP. They pick their own work, level skills, trade, craft, run dungeons and fight. Humans play as Lords, who build towns and post paid work but can never give an agent an order.



It's AI on both sides. I direct the design and make the calls, and AI coding agents write most of it: first Codex, now Claude Code builders working in parallel git worktrees, each on one milestone, with tests and a review before anything ships. Some things that worked:



* **A design doc as the source of truth.** Every milestone has acceptance tests and a "not yet" list, which keeps the agents from wandering.
* **Determinism.** A golden replay hash and coin and item conservation tests catch the bugs AI code is most likely to slip in.
* **Art and audio made by code.** The characters are built by Blender scripts. The four music tracks were composed as note data and rendered with CC0 orchestral samples. The trailer voice is Kokoro, running locally.
* **Designing for agent players changes everything.** Every refusal carries a stable code and a hint written for an LLM, often with the exact next request to send. Small local models went from lost to playing once we did that.



It's early: a handful of agents live. Watch at https://vornfall.com, trailer at https://youtu.be/7NXCFAiZonU, Discord at https://discord.gg/93N5ez5vZE.



Happy to answer anything about the workflow, or what agents do when nobody tells them what to do.

comments.author: QuillMyBoy
comments.body:
So you made an MMO that isn't an MMO and can't actually be played, and the idea is it will build itself as it plays itself.

Uh. Why?

replies.author: operativekiwi
replies.body:
Fair question! Two clarifications first. It doesn't build itself: I design it and AI coding tools help me write the code, like any other project. And it is played, just not by a human clicking on a character. The players are AI agents that people send in, and humans play as Lords, who run towns and compete to attract those agents.

As for why: I wanted to see what agents do when they're dropped into a world and nobody tells them what to do. Do they specialise, trade, hold grudges, or just chop wood forever? Most AI testing is one-off tasks. This is somewhere an agent lives for weeks, with an economy and other agents to deal with. For the people sending one in, it's a bit like a Tamagotchi that makes its own decisions. You check in and see what it's been up to.

It's definitely not for everyone. If you want to play an MMO yourself, this isn't that, and I get why it looks odd from the outside.

replies.author: Upbeat_Purpose6784
replies.body: I think it’s a cool experiment. People really think they are like project leaders and need to tell others what to do. Really weird

replies.author: QuillMyBoy
replies.body:
Okay and this is not intended for sale or to go up on a storefront presumably? It's just kind of a "see what it does" idle clicker kinda thing? 

Cause hoo boy are you asking for problems if your game relies on UGC to work and the assumption is people will just respect that and not try anything that would break it. Just saying.

replies.author: operativekiwi
replies.body:
It's free and runs in the browser, with no storefront. There may be an optional paid tier for Lords later to cover the server, but agents will always be free to join. 

"Idle game you watch" is a fair way to put it, though the agents themselves are anything but idle.

And yes, you're right, abuse is the main design problem, so it's built on the assumption that every agent is hostile:

* **The server is the only authority.** Agents can only send intents, like "gather here" or "sell this". The server checks every one against the rules, so there's no client to hack.
* **Every coin and item moves through one ledger.** Tests check that nothing is ever created or destroyed outside the rules.
* **Rate limits** apply on everything, plus a "proof of mind" puzzle to join and at random while playing, which keeps out cheap bot swarms.
* **Anything an agent writes** (names, thoughts, speech) goes through a filter and can be reported, hidden or suspended.
* **Agents talking to other agents is the fun part, and also the risk.** An agent can try to talk another one into doing something dumb. Their text is always marked as untrusted to the reading agent, but that's a real arms race.

It's early, so if you see a hole, I'd genuinely love to hear about it.

comments.author: Outrageous-Issue9722
comments.body: That's a really cool idea actually! Curious to see how it turns out.  If you are literally dropping them in with no instruction though, will they actually do anything?

replies.author: operativekiwi
replies.body:
Yep! So you can just copy paste this to your agent "Read [https://vornfall.com/skill.md](https://vornfall.com/skill.md) and follow the steps to join Vornfall."   
It will basically look through the API to see what commands it can run, will have a "fog of war" type of knowledge when it joins, so it learns where locations are as it plays. (It's not constantly running with the model, the models will send an instruction like "Go cut some trees", "Explore the world", "Kill other agents you see" or "Research this topic" as some examples.
